1.1.1:
Why this matters

"Six Sigma" is used three different ways, often in the same sentence. Exam questions take advantage of that. If you know which meaning a question intends, and you know the numbers behind the name, a whole family of questions becomes easy.

The big idea

Every process varies. No two deliveries take exactly the same time, no two bolts are exactly the same length. Customers set limits on how much variation they will accept. Six Sigma is about making the variation so small, compared with those limits, that defects almost never happen.

The name comes from a Greek letter. Sigma (σ) is the symbol statisticians use for the standard deviation, the typical distance of individual results from their average. A small σ means results are tightly bunched. A large σ means they are spread out.

Three meanings of "Six Sigma"

  1. A metric. A "six sigma process" produces about 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO). This is a performance level you can measure and compare.
  2. A methodology. Six Sigma is a structured way to solve problems, called DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. When someone says "we ran a Six Sigma project", they mean this.
  3. A management philosophy. Six Sigma is also a way to run an organization: decisions based on data, projects chosen for their effect on customers and the business, and trained people (the "belts") who lead the work.

When a question asks "what is Six Sigma?", the best answer usually includes all three. When it asks about 3.4 DPMO, it means the metric.

Sigma level: how many σ fit before the limit

Imagine measuring the weight of cereal boxes. The weights form a hill-shaped pattern called a normal distribution: most boxes are near the average, and fewer and fewer are far away from it. The customer (or the law) sets a specification limit, for example "no box above 56 g of air space" or "no delivery later than 5 days".

The sigma level asks one question: how many standard deviations fit between the process average and the nearest specification limit?

Z = (specification limit − process mean) ÷ σ

That number is called Z. If the mean is 50, σ is 2 and the upper limit is 56, then Z = (56 − 50) ÷ 2 = 3. Three standard deviations fit, so the process is at a sigma level of 3.

The farther the limit is from the mean, measured in σ steps, the smaller the tail of defects beyond it.

More room means fewer results land beyond the limit. Each extra σ of room cuts defects dramatically, because the tails of the normal curve shrink very fast.

You can get more σ of room in two ways: reduce the variation (make σ smaller, so more of them fit), or center the process (move the mean away from the limit it is crowding). That is why the goal of Six Sigma is reducing variation and centering the process. Inspecting finished products and throwing out the bad ones does neither. It only hides the problem and adds cost.

The 1.5σ shift: why 6σ means 3.4 per million

Here is the part that confuses almost everyone. If a process truly had six standard deviations of room on one side, the chance of a result beyond the limit would be about 1 in a billion on that side (about 0.002 parts per million counting both sides). So why does everyone say six sigma is 3.4 per million?

Because of a convention Motorola built into the definition. Motorola observed that processes measured over a short period look better than they really are over months and years. Over time the average drifts: new material lots, new operators, tool wear, seasons. Motorola assumed the average can drift about 1.5σ toward a limit in the long run.

Short-term data (solid) has full room to the limit. Over the long term the average drifts about 1.5σ (dashed), and many more results cross the limit.

So the convention says:

Long-term Z = short-term Z − 1.5

A process with 6σ of room in short-term data is expected to have only 4.5σ of room in the long run. The tail beyond 4.5σ is 3.4 per million. That is where the famous number comes from.

The sigma level that people report is the short-term figure (the 6). The DPMO they quote with it is the long-term expectation (the 3.4).

The anchor table

These are worth memorizing. They all include the 1.5σ shift.

Sigma levelLong-term ZDPMO (defects per million opportunities)Yield
20.5308,53869.1%
31.566,80793.3%
42.56,21099.38%
53.523399.977%
64.53.499.99966%

Notice how fast the defect rate falls. Going from 3 sigma to 4 sigma cuts defects by more than 10 times. Going from 5 to 6 cuts them by almost 70 times.

For contrast, with no shift (pure statistics), the area outside ±3σ is 0.27% (2,700 per million), outside ±4σ about 63 per million, and outside ±6σ about 0.002 per million.

Connecting sigma level to Cpk

You will meet a capability index called Cpk in Measure (2.4). It measures the same "room to the nearest limit", but in units of 3σ instead of σ:

Cpk = Z ÷ 3, so Z = 3 × Cpk

So Cpk 1.0 = 3 sigma, Cpk 1.33 = 4 sigma, Cpk 2.0 = 6 sigma. A Cpk of 1.33 therefore corresponds to about 6,210 DPMO in the long term (using the shift). The IASSC Reference Document states this relationship for attribute data as Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the long-term yield) ÷ 3, which is the same idea written the other way round: long-term Z plus 1.5 gives the short-term sigma level, and dividing by 3 gives Cpk.

Worked example

A trucking terminal loads trailers. The time to load has a mean of 40 minutes and a standard deviation of 4 minutes (from two weeks of data, so treat it as short-term). Dispatch needs every trailer loaded within 52 minutes.

  1. Room to the limit: 52 − 40 = 12 minutes.
  2. In σ units: Z = 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The process is at a 3 sigma level.
  3. Long-term expectation using the convention: long-term Z = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5. From the anchor table, about 66,807 late loads per million, or roughly 6.7%.
  4. Without the shift: the one-sided tail beyond Z = 3 is about 0.135%, or 1,350 per million. That is what the next two weeks would look like if nothing drifts.

Which answer is right? Both, under different assumptions. If a question uses words like "sigma level", "long-term" or "DPMO" and gives the 3.4 / 6,210 style numbers, use the shift. If it simply gives a mean, σ and a limit and asks for the expected fraction beyond the limit, use the Z table directly with no shift.

  1. How to reach 4 sigma: you need Z = 4, so 12 ÷ σ = 4, giving σ = 3 minutes. Alternatively, keep σ = 4 and move the mean to 52 − 16 = 36 minutes. Usually a project does some of each.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Mixing the two "six sigmas". "Six sigma = 3.4 DPMO" includes the shift. "Six sigma = ±6σ, about 0.002 ppm" does not. Read which one the question is using.
  • Adding the shift when you should not. If the question gives short-term σ and asks for expected defects without mentioning a shift or sigma level, use the Z table with no 1.5.
  • Thinking Six Sigma means inspecting harder. Inspection catches defects after they are made. Six Sigma reduces variation so they are not made.
  • Forgetting the nearest limit. With two limits, the sigma level is set by the closer one, because that is where the defects come from.

Check yourself

  1. Name the three meanings of Six Sigma.
  2. A process has mean 100, σ = 5, and an upper limit of 115 (no lower limit). What is its sigma level?
  3. Why is a six sigma process said to make 3.4 DPMO instead of about 0.002 ppm?
  4. A process runs at 6,210 DPMO. What sigma level is that, and what Cpk?
  5. Two teams improve the same process. One cuts σ in half. The other moves the mean away from the limit by 1σ. Which gains more sigma level if the process started at Z = 3?
Show answers
  1. A metric (3.4 DPMO), a methodology (DMAIC), and a management philosophy (data-driven, project-based improvement).
  2. Z = (115 − 100) ÷ 5 = 3, so a 3 sigma level.
  3. The convention assumes the long-term mean drifts 1.5σ toward the limit, so a short-term 6σ process has 4.5σ of long-term room, and the tail beyond 4.5σ is 3.4 per million.
  4. 4 sigma, and Cpk = 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.33.
  5. Halving σ doubles Z from 3 to 6, a gain of 3. Moving the mean 1σ gains only 1 (Z = 4). Cutting variation is far more powerful here.

Key takeaways

  • Six Sigma is a metric, a method (DMAIC), and a philosophy.
  • Sigma level = how many σ fit between the mean and the nearest spec limit.
  • The 1.5σ shift convention turns a short-term 6σ into 3.4 DPMO long-term.
  • Memorize: 2σ = 308,538; 3σ = 66,807; 4σ = 6,210; 5σ = 233; 6σ = 3.4 DPMO.
  • Cpk = Z ÷ 3, so Cpk 1.33 = 4σ.
  • The goal is less variation and better centering, not more inspection.
1.1.2:
Why this matters

Six Sigma did not appear from nowhere. Almost every tool in it was invented by someone between the 1920s and the 1990s. The exam asks matching questions: which person gave us which idea, and what came first. Learning the story makes these easy, because each idea grew out of the one before.

The big idea

The history has three strands that eventually merged:

  1. Statistical quality control (Shewhart, Deming): use statistics to understand and reduce variation.
  2. Quality management (Juran, Feigenbaum, Crosby, Ishikawa, Taguchi): make quality a management responsibility and count what poor quality costs.
  3. Lean (Toyota: Toyoda, Ohno, Shingo): remove waste and make work flow.

Motorola combined strand 1 and 2 into Six Sigma in 1986. In the 2000s, companies merged it with strand 3 to make Lean Six Sigma.

The quality pioneers, in order

Walter Shewhart (1920s, Bell Laboratories). Shewhart realized that all processes vary, and that there are two kinds of variation: the routine background kind that is always present, and unusual variation that has a specific cause. In 1924 he invented the control chart to tell them apart. He also described a cycle of learning (plan, do, check, act) that later became famous. Shewhart is the father of statistical quality control.

W. Edwards Deming (1950s onward). A student of Shewhart's ideas, Deming taught statistical quality methods to Japanese industry from 1950, and Japan's quality revolution followed. He popularized the PDCA cycle (he preferred PDSA: Plan, Do, Study, Act), named the two kinds of variation common cause and special cause, and wrote 14 Points for Management, which say that most quality problems come from the system that management designs, not from the workers. Japan's top quality award is the Deming Prize.

Joseph Juran (1950s onward). Juran wrote the Quality Control Handbook (1951) and focused on management. His Quality Trilogy says quality takes three processes: quality planning, quality control, and quality improvement. He applied the Pareto principle to quality (the "vital few and trivial many") and pushed companies to measure the cost of poor quality in money, the language executives understand.

Armand Feigenbaum (1950s). Feigenbaum coined Total Quality Control: quality is everyone's job across the whole company, from design to sales, not just the inspection department. He also described the "hidden plant", the share of a factory's capacity spent fixing mistakes.

Kaoru Ishikawa (1950s to 1960s, Japan). Ishikawa created the cause-and-effect diagram, also called the fishbone or Ishikawa diagram, and promoted quality circles: small groups of workers who meet to solve problems in their own area. He also championed the "seven basic quality tools" for everyday problem solving.

Philip Crosby (1979). Crosby wrote Quality Is Free, arguing that preventing defects costs less than fixing them, so quality pays for itself. He promoted zero defects as a performance standard and defined quality as conformance to requirements.

Genichi Taguchi (1960s to 1980s, Japan). Taguchi introduced the quality loss function: any deviation from the target value causes some loss, even inside the specification limits, and the loss grows quickly the farther you go. He also developed robust design: designing products and processes that perform well even when conditions vary.

Toyota and the roots of Lean

Sakichi Toyoda built automatic looms in the early 1900s that stopped by themselves when a thread broke. This idea, building quality into the machine so it never produces defects silently, is called jidoka.

Taiichi Ohno developed the Toyota Production System (TPS) from the late 1940s through the 1970s: just-in-time production, pull systems, kanban and waste elimination.

Shigeo Shingo worked with Toyota on SMED (single-minute exchange of die, fast changeovers) and poka-yoke (mistake-proofing).

Lean is covered in depth in 1.4.

Motorola invents Six Sigma

In the early 1980s Motorola was losing market share to higher-quality Japanese competitors. CEO Bob Galvin demanded dramatic improvement. In 1986 engineer Bill Smith proposed the Six Sigma standard (3.4 defects per million opportunities), and Mikel Harry developed much of the structured, statistics-based problem-solving approach and the belt training system. Motorola won the first Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award in 1988, which made its methods famous.

AlliedSignal and GE scale it up

Larry Bossidy brought Six Sigma to AlliedSignal in the early 1990s. Jack Welch made it company-wide at General Electric from 1995, tying managers' bonuses to it and publicizing large savings. GE's success turned Six Sigma into a global business movement.

Lean Six Sigma and standards

In the late 1990s and 2000s companies combined Six Sigma (variation and defects) with Lean (waste and speed) into Lean Six Sigma. In 2011 the international standard ISO 13053 described the DMAIC methodology, giving it a formal reference. It is rarely tested.

A timeline to remember

Memory hooks

  • Shewhart = Sheets of control charts. The first statistician of quality.
  • Deming = Do (PDSA) and Doctrine (14 points).
  • Juran = Journey of three (trilogy) and Junk costs (cost of poor quality).
  • Crosby = Costs nothing ("Quality Is Free"), zero defects.
  • Ishikawa = Image of a fish.
  • Taguchi = Target (loss grows away from target).
  • Feigenbaum = Full company (total quality control).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Deming vs Shewhart on PDCA. Shewhart described the cycle; Deming popularized it (as PDSA). If asked who is associated with PDCA, Deming is the usual answer.
  • Juran vs Pareto. Vilfredo Pareto was an economist who noticed that 80% of land was owned by 20% of people. Juran applied the idea to quality problems.
  • Motorola vs GE. Motorola created Six Sigma (1986). GE did not invent it; GE scaled it.
  • Crosby vs Deming on zero defects. Zero defects is Crosby. Deming actually criticized slogans and targets like that.

Check yourself

  1. Who invented the control chart, and where?
  2. What are the three parts of Juran's trilogy?
  3. Which pioneer said any deviation from target creates loss, even within specification?
  4. Put in order: GE adopts Six Sigma, Shewhart's control chart, Motorola creates Six Sigma, Baldrige Award to Motorola.
  5. What is jidoka, and who started it?
Show answers
  1. Walter Shewhart, at Bell Laboratories in the 1920s (1924).
  2. Quality planning, quality control and quality improvement.
  3. Genichi Taguchi (the quality loss function).
  4. Shewhart's control chart (1924), Motorola creates Six Sigma (1986), Baldrige Award to Motorola (1988), GE adopts Six Sigma (1995).
  5. Building quality in by making a machine stop automatically when something goes wrong. Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping loom.

Key takeaways

  • Statistical control (Shewhart, Deming) + quality management (Juran, Feigenbaum, Crosby, Ishikawa, Taguchi) + Lean (Toyota) = Lean Six Sigma.
  • Shewhart: control chart. Deming: PDSA, 14 points, common vs special cause. Juran: trilogy, Pareto, cost of quality. Crosby: zero defects. Ishikawa: fishbone. Taguchi: loss function. Feigenbaum: total quality control.
  • Motorola 1986 (Bill Smith, Mikel Harry), Baldrige 1988; AlliedSignal (Bossidy) and GE (Welch, 1995) scaled it.
1.1.3:
Why this matters

A Six Sigma project is not "work on the problem until it feels fixed". It moves through five phases, and each phase must produce specific outputs, called deliverables, before the next phase starts. Knowing what belongs where keeps a project honest, and the exam asks it directly.

The big idea

DMAIC works like a funnel of evidence:

  • Define says what the problem is and why it matters.
  • Measure says how big it really is, with trustworthy data.
  • Analyze proves what is causing it.
  • Improve fixes the proven causes and shows the fix works.
  • Control makes sure it stays fixed after the team walks away.

Skipping a phase is the most common way projects fail. Teams that jump from Define straight to Improve end up fixing what they guessed, not what the data shows.

Deliverables, phase by phase

Define: agree on the problem.

  • Project charter, signed by the sponsor: business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team, timeline (see 1.3.1).
  • SIPOC: a one-page, high-level map of Suppliers, Inputs, Process steps, Outputs and Customers (see 2.1.2).
  • Voice of the customer (VOC) and the list of CTQs (critical-to-quality requirements) it produces (see 1.1.5 and 1.2.2).
  • Stakeholder map: who is affected, who must support it.

Measure: get the facts.

  • Data collection plan: what to measure, how, how often, by whom.
  • Validated measurement system (MSA): proof that the measurements themselves are trustworthy (see 2.3).
  • Baseline performance: how the process performs today (for example DPMO, yield, cycle time).
  • Baseline capability: how well today's process fits the customer's limits (Cp, Cpk, sigma level, see 2.4).

Analyze: find and prove the root causes.

  • List of potential causes (from fishbones, process maps, brainstorming).
  • Statistically validated root causes: the "vital few X's" proven with data, using hypothesis tests, regression and similar tools (see Domain 3).

Improve: fix the causes and prove the fix.

  • Selected solutions that address the proven causes.
  • Pilot results: the solution tested on a small scale, with before-and-after data.
  • Updated FMEA: risks of the new process reviewed (see 2.1.4).
  • Implementation plan for full rollout.

Control: lock in the gain.

  • Control plan: what will be monitored, how, how often, by whom (see 5.3).
  • Response plan: what to do if the process drifts.
  • Standard work and training updated.
  • Handoff to the process owner, who now owns the improved process.
  • Financial sign-off of the benefits and project closure.

Tollgate reviews

At the end of each phase the team meets the sponsor or champion in a tollgate review (sometimes called a phase-gate). The team presents the deliverables. The sponsor decides: proceed, revisit, or stop. A phase is finished only when its deliverables are accepted. Tollgates keep management involved, catch weak evidence early, and let the organization stop projects that are no longer worth doing.

Hard and soft benefits at closure

When the project closes, benefits are reported in two kinds:

  • Hard benefits: money that shows up on the financial statements, such as lower scrap, less overtime or fewer freight claims.
  • Soft benefits: real but harder to put in the bank, such as freed-up capacity, better customer satisfaction, cost avoidance or improved safety.

More in 1.3.3.

Worked example

A carrier wants to reduce damaged freight claims. Which phase does each item belong to?

ItemPhaseWhy
"Claims cost $480k last year; goal is to halve them by Q4"DefinePart of the charter (business case and goal)
Gauge study confirming dock inspectors classify damage consistentlyMeasureValidating the measurement system
Current rate of 3.1 claims per 1,000 loadsMeasureBaseline performance
Regression showing claims rise with trailers loaded in under 25 minutesAnalyzeStatistically validated root cause
New load-securing procedure trialed at one terminal for 6 weeksImprovePilot
Weekly chart of claims per 1,000 loads with a reaction planControlControl and response plan

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Baseline capability belongs to Measure, not Define. Define says the problem exists and matters. Measure quantifies it.
  • "Root causes" are Analyze deliverables only when validated with data. A brainstormed fishbone alone is a list of suspects, not proof.
  • The pilot is Improve, not Control. Control comes after the solution is proven and rolled out.
  • The process owner takes over in Control. The Green Belt does not keep running the process.

Check yourself

  1. In which phase do you validate the measurement system?
  2. What is a tollgate review, and who decides whether the project passes?
  3. A team presents a fishbone diagram with 25 possible causes. Has it completed Analyze?
  4. Name two Control-phase deliverables.
  5. Is "reduced overtime, saving $60k this year" a hard or soft benefit?
Show answers
  1. Measure.
  2. A review at the end of each phase where the team presents its deliverables; the sponsor or champion decides to proceed, revisit or stop.
  3. No. It has potential causes. Analyze ends only when the vital few causes are validated with data.
  4. Any two of: control plan, response plan, updated standard work and training, handoff to the process owner, financial sign-off.
  5. Hard. It is real money on the financial statements.

Key takeaways

  • Define: charter, SIPOC, VOC/CTQs, stakeholders.
  • Measure: data collection plan, validated measurement system, baseline performance and capability.
  • Analyze: statistically validated root causes.
  • Improve: piloted solution, updated FMEA, implementation plan.
  • Control: control plan, response plan, handoff, financial sign-off.
  • A phase ends when the sponsor accepts its deliverables at a tollgate.
1.1.4:
Why this matters

"Y = f(X)" is the single idea that ties all of Six Sigma together. Every phase of DMAIC is a step in finding and controlling the X's that drive a Y. Once you see a process this way, the tools make sense: each one either measures the Y, finds the X's, or controls them.

The big idea

Any result you care about depends on the things that go into producing it.

Y = f(X₁, X₂, X₃, …, Xₙ) + error

Read it as: the output (Y) is a function of the inputs (X's), plus some leftover variation we cannot explain.

Think about a truck's fuel economy. That is your Y. What does it depend on? Speed, tire pressure, load weight, idling time, route terrain, weather, the engine's condition and the driver's habits. Those are the X's. If fuel economy is bad, staring at the fuel gauge will not fix it. You have to find which X's are responsible and change them.

Vocabulary for Y and X

The same two ideas have many names. Learn them as pairs:

The YThe X
OutputInput
ResponseFactor, driver
EffectCause
Dependent variableIndependent variable
CTQ (what the customer cares about)Process variable
SymptomRoot cause

The vital few

A process may have dozens of X's, but usually only a few of them cause most of the variation in Y. These are the vital few; the rest are the trivial many. Much of the Measure and Analyze work is narrowing a long list of suspect X's down to the vital few, using data. This is the same 80/20 thinking as the Pareto principle (see 1.2.4).

Monitor the Y, control the X's

If Y depends on the X's, then the way to control Y is to control the X's. Measuring Y tells you whether there is a problem. Controlling the X's prevents it.

  • A thermostat does not control your comfort directly; it controls the furnace (an X), and comfort (the Y) follows.
  • Checking every trailer's damage at delivery (Y) finds damage after the fact. Controlling load securing and driving behavior (X's) prevents it.

This is why the Control phase sets up controls on the critical X's, while still watching Y to confirm it stays good.

Four steps from problem to solution

Six Sigma moves a problem through a statistical "translation" and back:

  1. Practical problem: "Too many late deliveries."
  2. Statistical problem: "On-time rate is 87% with high day-to-day variation; the target is 97%."
  3. Statistical solution: "Data shows 70% of late deliveries are explained by departure delays at two terminals and by route length over 400 miles."
  4. Practical solution: "Change dock scheduling at those two terminals and add a relay point on long routes."

The middle two steps are where data replaces opinion.

Types of inputs: C, N, P and X

When teams list inputs (on a process map or fishbone), they often tag each one:

  • C, controllable: you can set it and hold it, such as oven temperature or dispatch time.
  • N, noise: it affects Y but is hard or too expensive to control, such as weather, traffic or humidity. You design around it instead.
  • P, procedural (SOP): controlled by a written procedure, such as "inspect straps before departure".
  • X, critical: an input proven by data to be one of the vital few. (Some materials use "X" for any input; in this classification it marks the critical ones.)

Worked example

A distribution center's problem: picking errors (wrong item shipped). The team lists these candidates. Which is the Y, and how would you tag the inputs?

  • Number of picking errors per 1,000 order lines
  • Picker experience (months)
  • Shelf label layout
  • Lighting in the aisle
  • Daily order volume
  • The written pick-and-check procedure

The Y is picking errors per 1,000 order lines. It is the measurable outcome the customer feels.

Inputs: picker experience (C, the company controls hiring and training), shelf label layout (C), aisle lighting (C), daily order volume (N, set by customers, not controllable), pick-and-check procedure (P). After analysis, if regression shows label layout and experience explain most of the errors, those two become the critical X's.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Picking a cause as the Y. In "which is the Y?" questions, the Y is the measurable outcome (errors, time, cost, satisfaction), not something that causes it.
  • Trying to fix the Y directly. Rework, inspection and expediting attack the Y. Lasting fixes change the X's.
  • Treating noise as controllable. You cannot control the weather; you can make the process robust to it.

Check yourself

  1. In Y = f(X), which one is the dependent variable?
  2. A bakery's complaint rate depends on oven temperature, flour supplier, humidity and baking time. Which of these is most likely noise?
  3. Why does Six Sigma say "control the X's" instead of "inspect the Y"?
  4. Put in order: statistical solution, practical problem, practical solution, statistical problem.
  5. A hospital measures patient wait time. Is "number of nurses on shift" a Y or an X?
Show answers
  1. Y.
  2. Humidity, because it affects results but is hard to control.
  3. Because Y is the result of the X's. Controlling the inputs prevents problems; inspecting the output only finds them after they happen.
  4. Practical problem, statistical problem, statistical solution, practical solution.
  5. An X: it is an input that influences wait time.

Key takeaways

  • Y = f(X) + error: outputs depend on inputs.
  • Y = output, effect, response, CTQ. X = input, cause, factor.
  • A few X's (the vital few) drive most of the variation.
  • Monitor the Y, control the X's.
  • Practical problem, statistical problem, statistical solution, practical solution.
  • Inputs: controllable, noise, procedural, and critical (proven vital few).
1.1.5:
Why this matters

A project that improves something the customer does not care about is wasted effort. Six Sigma starts by listening: to customers, to the business, and to the people doing the work. Then it turns what they say, which is usually vague, into measurable requirements.

The big idea

There are three "voices" a project must hear:

  • Voice of the Customer (VOC): what the external customer needs and expects. "My delivery has to arrive on the day you promised."
  • Voice of the Business (VOB): what the organization needs: profit, cost, growth, regulatory compliance, return on investment. "We must cut fuel cost per mile by 8%."
  • Voice of the Employee (VOE): what the people doing the work need: safety, tools, training, reasonable workload. "We cannot meet the schedule with two forklifts down."

A good project balances all three. Satisfying customers in a way that bankrupts the business, or burns out employees, is not a success.

Where VOC comes from

There are two styles of listening:

Reactive sources: information that arrives on its own, usually when something went wrong.

  • Complaints, returns, warranty claims, credit notes, customer service calls, online reviews.
  • Cheap to collect, but biased: you mainly hear from unhappy customers, and only about problems they notice.

Proactive sources: information you go out and get.

  • Surveys: reach many customers; good for measuring how many feel a certain way.
  • Interviews: one-to-one, deep understanding of needs and reasons.
  • Focus groups: small group discussion; good for exploring ideas.
  • Observation / gemba walks: watching customers use the product or service where it happens ("gemba" means "the real place"). Reveals needs customers never say.
  • CRM and transaction data: what customers actually do, not what they say.

The best VOC combines both: reactive data shows where pain is, proactive methods explain why.

Turning a vague voice into a CTQ

Customers speak in general terms: "fast", "easy", "reliable", "friendly". You cannot measure "fast". So the team translates each statement in three steps, using a CTQ tree:

  1. Need: the general want. "Fast delivery."
  2. Drivers: what "fast" means to them, broken into specifics. "Order ships the same day", "Truck arrives on the promised day".
  3. CTQ: a measurable requirement with a target and a limit. "Order placed by 2 p.m. ships the same day (target 100%, at least 98%)"; "Delivery within the promised day (no later than 6 p.m.)".

A CTQ has a measure, a target and a limit. More on CTQs in 1.2.2.

The Kano model: not all needs are equal

Professor Noriaki Kano showed that customer needs behave differently. Picture a chart: the horizontal axis is how well you deliver a feature, the vertical axis is customer satisfaction.

Must-be (basic) needs. Expected so completely that customers do not even mention them: brakes that work, freight that is not damaged, an invoice with the right price. Delivering them perfectly earns no praise; failing them causes strong dissatisfaction. They can only stop customers being unhappy.

One-dimensional (performance) needs. More is better, less is worse, in a roughly straight line: faster delivery, lower price, better fuel economy. Customers talk about these openly and compare competitors on them.

Attractive (delighter) needs. Customers do not expect them, so their absence causes no dissatisfaction, but their presence delights: live GPS tracking with a photo at delivery, a driver who calls ahead unasked. These create loyalty.

Two more categories exist:

  • Indifferent: customers do not care either way.
  • Reverse: some customers actively dislike it (for example, too many notification texts).

Needs move over time. Yesterday's delighter becomes today's performance need and tomorrow's must-be. Shipment tracking delighted customers once; now it is expected.

QFD and the House of Quality

Quality Function Deployment (QFD) is a structured way to connect customer requirements ("whats") to technical design characteristics ("hows"). Its main chart, the House of Quality, is a matrix with customer needs down the side, technical characteristics across the top, relationship strengths inside, and a triangular "roof" showing how the technical characteristics affect each other. It is mostly used in product design and is lightly tested.

Worked example

A freight broker surveys shippers. Classify each statement with Kano:

StatementKano categoryWhy
"The truck must show up."Must-beExpected; failure is a disaster, success earns nothing
"The cheaper the rate, the better."One-dimensionalSatisfaction rises steadily as price falls
"I loved that you texted a photo of the signed delivery receipt."AttractiveUnexpected, creates delight
"I don't care which brand of truck you use."IndifferentNo effect on satisfaction

Now translate "I want to know where my freight is" into a CTQ. Need: visibility. Driver: location updates while in transit. CTQ: "Location update posted at least every 2 hours while the load is moving (target: 100% of loads)".

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Over-delivering a must-be. Making must-be quality even better does not create delight; it only prevents dissatisfaction. Spend effort on performance and attractive needs once basics are reliable.
  • Treating complaints as complete VOC. Complaints are reactive and biased toward unhappy, vocal customers.
  • Stopping at the vague voice. "Fast" is not a CTQ. It needs a measure, a target and a limit.
  • Forgetting VOB and VOE. A solution customers love but the business cannot afford is not acceptable.

Check yourself

  1. What are the three voices, and give one example of each.
  2. Is analyzing returned products a reactive or proactive VOC source?
  3. A hotel guest is not pleased by clean sheets, but is furious if they are dirty. Which Kano category?
  4. What three elements does a well-written CTQ contain?
  5. Why might a delighter stop delighting?
Show answers
  1. VOC (customer: on-time delivery), VOB (business: lower cost per mile), VOE (employees: working equipment and safety).
  2. Reactive.
  3. Must-be (basic).
  4. A measure, a target and a limit (specification).
  5. Customers get used to it, so it becomes expected (a performance or must-be need).

Key takeaways

  • VOC = customer, VOB = business, VOE = employees; balance all three.
  • Reactive sources (complaints, returns) vs proactive sources (surveys, interviews, observation).
  • Translate vague needs into measurable CTQs: need, then drivers, then CTQ.
  • Kano: must-be (only dissatisfies), one-dimensional (more is better), attractive (only delights); plus indifferent and reverse.
  • Needs drift over time from delighter to must-be.
1.1.6:
Why this matters

Improvement projects fail more often for organizational reasons (no time, no resources, no support) than technical ones. Six Sigma assigns clear roles so that someone owns every part of making a project succeed. The exam asks who does what, especially who to go to when the team is blocked.

The big idea

Think of a project like a long-haul delivery:

  • The shipper (sponsor) pays for it and cares about the result.
  • Dispatch (champion) clears the way: permits, routes, problems with other departments.
  • The driver (belt) does the work.
  • The receiver (process owner) takes ownership at the end.
  • A trainer (Master Black Belt) taught the driver and helps on hard routes.

The roles

Executive leadership. Sets the strategy, decides that the organization will use Six Sigma, and makes it part of how the business is run. Without visible executive support, programs fade.

Sponsor. A senior manager who owns the business result the project affects. The sponsor funds the project, provides resources, signs the charter, and accepts the deliverables at tollgates. The sponsor is accountable for the result.

Champion. A manager who links projects to strategy and removes organizational barriers: getting people released from other duties, resolving conflicts with other departments, getting decisions made. In many organizations the sponsor and champion are the same person; when they are separate, the champion often oversees several projects and helps choose them.

Process owner. The person who owns the process day to day. They help define the problem, and at the end they take over the improved process and its control plan. If the process owner is not involved, improvements tend to disappear after the team leaves.

Master Black Belt (MBB). The organization's Six Sigma expert. Trains and coaches Black Belts and Green Belts, helps with difficult statistics, reviews project quality, and often helps run the overall program.

Black Belt (BB). Usually full-time on improvement. Leads larger, cross-functional projects, uses advanced statistics, and mentors Green Belts.

Green Belt (GB). Usually part-time: keeps their regular job and leads smaller projects within their own area, or works on a Black Belt's team. Knows the core tools of DMAIC and basic statistics.

Yellow Belt and White Belt. Basic awareness. Yellow Belts usually serve as team members, collect data and help with tasks; White Belts know the vocabulary and support local improvements.

Team members. People who work in the process. They bring knowledge of how the work really happens, which no expert can replace.

Summary table

RoleTime on projectsMain job
SponsorPartOwns the result, funds it, signs the charter
ChampionPartRemoves barriers, aligns to strategy
Process ownerPartOwns the process, takes over at the end
Master Black BeltFullTrains, coaches, runs the program
Black BeltFullLeads big projects, advanced analysis
Green BeltPartLeads smaller projects in own area
Yellow / White BeltPartTeam support, basic tools

Worked example

A Green Belt's project to reduce invoice errors needs two people from the billing department for four hours a week, but the billing manager refuses to release them. Who should solve this?

Not the Green Belt: they have no authority over another department's staff. This is an organizational barrier, so it goes to the champion (or sponsor), who can negotiate with the billing manager or escalate.

After the project, who makes sure invoice errors stay low? The process owner for invoicing, using the control plan the team hands over.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • "Who removes the roadblock?" The champion or sponsor, never the Green Belt.
  • "Who signs the charter?" The sponsor (often with the champion and process owner).
  • "Who owns the process after the project?" The process owner, not the belt.
  • Black Belt vs Green Belt. Full-time vs part-time; cross-functional vs own area; advanced vs core statistics.

Check yourself

  1. Who trains and mentors Black Belts?
  2. Which role usually works on improvement part-time while keeping their regular job?
  3. Who takes over the control plan at project closure?
  4. A team cannot get access to data held by another department. Who should they escalate to?
  5. What is the difference between a sponsor and a process owner?
Show answers
  1. The Master Black Belt.
  2. The Green Belt.
  3. The process owner.
  4. The champion (or sponsor).
  5. The sponsor owns the business result and funds the project; the process owner runs the process day to day and keeps the improvement in place afterward.

Key takeaways

  • Sponsor: owns results, funds, signs the charter. Champion: removes barriers, aligns to strategy.
  • Process owner: owns the process and its control plan after the project.
  • MBB trains and coaches; BB leads big projects full-time; GB leads smaller projects part-time in their own area.
  • Escalate organizational roadblocks to the champion or sponsor.
